# Introduction

Basketball players have traditionally been described by five positions, yet game-related statistics only partly separate these positions [@sampaio2006discriminant], and a growing literature replaces them with data-driven functional roles [@kalman2020lineup; @ibanez2025redefining; @chen2023modeling; @wei2025enhancing; @pendolareinecke2025exploring; @south2024basketball; @courelibanez2025profiling]. At the same time, the game itself has changed: three-point attempts have risen steadily in the NBA [@zajac2023long], where a distinct modern era has been described since 2013 [@silva2021three], and in the leading European leagues [@nietoacevedo2025modern], with the EuroLeague relying more on three-point shooting than the NBA [@foteinakis2025decade]; within-position variability has increased [@durmus2026from], and player profiles migrate between archetypes from season to season [@madeira2026tempo]. Whether these changes have dissolved positions into roles, as the notion of "positionless" basketball implies, has rarely been tested with a fixed and reproducible role definition. The number of roles reported varies widely between studies, and a recent systematic review attributed these differences largely to methodological heterogeneity and called for a unified, high-quality approach [@ribes2026identifying]. In the EuroLeague, data-driven work has documented the convergence of power forwards and centres [@konca2026from] and has modelled lineups with regularised plus-minus [@grassetti2020extended], but a stability-tested taxonomy of player roles for the men's competition has not been reported; existing EuroLeague role studies concern the women's competition [@pendolareinecke2025exploring] or specific skills such as shooting [@vazquezguerrero2026shooting].

Two methodological gaps limit what role studies can claim. First, the number of roles is usually chosen with internal validity indices [@duman2021cluster], whereas the reproducibility of the partition under resampling [@hennig2007cluster; @lange2004stability; @luxburg2010clustering] is seldom reported, and resampling rarely respects the fact that the same players appear in several seasons. Second, roles are frequently linked to team or lineup success [@kalman2020lineup; @chen2023modeling; @penner2025player], but lineup outcomes are noisy, lineups are short-lived, and the players who make up a successful role combination are often simply better players. Because lineup performance can be predicted from the quality of the individual players [@martonosi2023predicting], role effects need to be evaluated after player quality has been accounted for.

The aims of this study were therefore (1) to derive functional player roles for the EuroLeague from open data, choosing the number of roles by player-level bootstrap stability; (2) to quantify how far these roles cut across registered positions and whether this changed between 2016 and 2024; and (3) to test whether the role composition of a lineup explains its performance beyond the individual quality of its players. Here we show that four or five roles can be recovered reproducibly, whereas finer partitions cannot; that ball handlers and rim protectors remain largely tied to registered positions whereas the other roles combine positions, and that no change in this structure was detected over nine seasons; and that an apparent effect of role composition on lineup performance beyond player quality is not robust once role information from the test period is excluded.
